## The city's taxable sales

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| County taxable sales, average of sales tax years 2022–23 to 2024–25 | \$`r fb(B_k)` billion |
| City, raw division of the county figure (@sec-apportionment) | \$`r fb(B_pred)` billion (`r fp(B_pred / B_k)` of county) |
| **City, after calibration (@sec-calibration)** | **\$`r fb(est_pref$B_c_central)` billion (`r fp(s_cal)` of county)** |
| 68% range (two chances in three) | \$`r fb(est_pref$lo68)`–`r fb(est_pref$hi68)` billion |
| 90% range | \$`r fb(est_pref$lo90)`–`r fb(est_pref$hi90)` billion |
| Same share applied to the latest year (`r R$latest_label`, \$`r fb(R$B_latest)` billion) | \$`r fb(s_cal * R$B_latest)` billion |
| Concentration ratio R (city share of sales ÷ city share of population) | `r f2(R_cal)` |

## Revenue

| Measure | \$ million a year |
|---|---:|
| **Central estimate, `r R$years_label` activity levels** | **`r fm(REV)`** |
| Central estimate at `r R$latest_label` levels | `r fm(rev(s_cal * R$B_latest))` |
| 68% range | `r fm(rev(est_pref$lo68))` – `r fm(rev(est_pref$hi68))` |
| 90% range | `r fm(rev(est_pref$lo90))` – `r fm(rev(est_pref$hi90))` |
| If no calibration cities are excluded | `r fm(REV_all)` |
| With a 3% shopping loss | `r fm(rev(est_pref$B_c_central, 0.97))` |

The county base grew `r fp(R$cagr, 1)` a year from 2022–23 to 2025–26 (`r fp(R$by_year$growth[R$by_year$fy == 2026], 1)` in the latest year). For a tax starting in 2027 or later, the estimate should be read as a share, `r fp(s_cal)` of whatever the county base then is, rather than as a fixed dollar figure.

## Where Albany sits among cities that tax

Seventeen taxing cities have an observed concentration ratio R ranging from `r f2(min(route_b$R))` (Yonkers) to `r f2(max(route_b$R))` (Oneida), median `r f2(median(route_b$R))`. Albany's calibrated R of `r f2(R_cal)` sits just below the median, next to `r paste(route_b$city[order(abs(route_b$R - R_cal))][1:3], collapse = ", ")`. That is the expected shape: a city whose retail has moved to the suburbs (its retail-only R is `r f2(R$a_ecret / pop)`) but which holds `r fp(R$a_wxp)` of the county's private-sector jobs. The two Albany quantities that can be observed directly bracket the answer: the retail-receipts share (`r fp(R$a_ecret)`) below and the measured utility share (`r fp(R$a_util)`) above, with the estimate at `r fp(s_cal)` between them.

## A reasonable range, and how it relates to the statistical one

Two ranges are reported and they should not be confused.

The **statistical range** (68%: \$`r fm(rev(est_pref$lo68))`–`r fm(rev(est_pref$hi68))` million; 90%: \$`r fm(rev(est_pref$lo90))`–`r fm(rev(est_pref$hi90))` million) comes from how far the method missed on the calibration cities. It treats Albany as no easier to predict than any of them. It is the honest statement of how well the method performs where it can be checked, at the point estimate of the typical miss.

The **planning range of \$`r R$PLAN_LO`–`r R$PLAN_HI` million** is computed rather than chosen. It is the envelope of two things: the 68% range evaluated at the *upper* end of the confidence interval for the typical miss itself (σ is known only to within `r f3(s_ci["lo"])`–`r f3(s_ci["hi"])` on 13 degrees of freedom, and at its upper end the 68% range is \$`r fm(rev(est_pref$B_c_central * exp(-s_ci["hi"])))`–`r fm(rev(est_pref$B_c_central * exp(s_ci["hi"])))` million); and every plausible specification tried in @sec-sensitivity: which cities are included, the form of the calibration line, and the sharing rule for sales to businesses. Three observations bear on how to read it:

1. The statistical range understates the uncertainty in two ways the envelope partly repairs. The typical miss is estimated from fifteen residuals and is itself uncertain by a factor of about 1.6 either way. And `r fp(R$cty_fe, 0)` of the miss is *between counties*, so Albany is a fresh draw from a distribution of county effects estimated on only eleven counties.
2. Discrete choices sit outside the statistical range entirely. On the same fifteen cities, fixing the calibration line's slope at one instead of estimating it gives \$`r fm(rev(grid[["Slope fixed at 1"]][2]))` million against \$`r fm(REV)` million, and the plausible business sharing rules span \$`r fm(min(af$rev[!af$key %in% c("lodes", "residence")]))`–`r fm(max(af$rev[!af$key %in% c("lodes", "residence")]))` million (@sec-apportionment).
3. Albany's sharing rules resolve at fine industry detail, its Economic Census coverage is near-complete, and its one measurable component lies between the two jobs rules. These are conditions under which the method should do better than its average, though nothing in the data proves it.

::: {.keypoint}
If a single figure is needed for budgeting, **\$`r R$BUDGET` million** is the prudent choice at steady state and current activity levels: the central estimate rounded down, inside every plausible specification tried, and above the residence-only floor. The first year will be lower for reasons that have nothing to do with the base (@sec-timing).
:::
